newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FROM THE HILL-Invertebrate backbone of NZ campaign.
newsitem.headline: FROM THE HILL-Invertebrate backbone of NZ campaign.

text.p: Things have come to a sorry pass when the noble art of political punditry is replaced by a low-tech invertebrate.

But with only three more big sleeps until New Zealanders go to the polls, policies, likely coalitions, even leadership has taken a temporary backseat to Television New Zealand's "worm" -- an electronic wriggly line which measures a studio audience of undecided voters reaction to the leaders' performance.
Last week the worm befriended Labour leader Helen Clark and her campaign received a huge boost.
Her standing as preferred prime minister has quadrupled from around four percent to 17 percent.

Even without the worm it was obvious that Prime Minister Jim Bolger had turned in a poor performance. No one can say "death is always associated with health care" and be crushed in the stampede of swinging voters.
But the worm was unequivocally convinced by Clark.
Bolger and his team cried foul and unsuccessfully tried to have the worm squashed for the replay.
On Monday the worm had its second outing and Clark got the nod once more.

Bolger again "wormed" poorly despite a much more assured performance. According to the 120 worm-drivers 37.4 percent voted Clark a winner, Anderton was second on 36.5 and Bolger had 16.5 percent. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters came last with 9.6 percent and his party president stamped on the worm describing it as "irrelevant and misleading".
Other leaders have criticised the worm and political scientists have lamented the focus on it at the expense of "more important" campaign issues.

Now, without wanting to anthropomorphise the worm any more than it already has been, it is clear that an "undecided" worm does not have the characteristics of a traditional undecided voter. In a strange way, it has already made up its "mind".
Whenever Clark and Anderton spoke it seemed to rise. Whenever Bolger spoke, even saying things which were remarkably similar to the other two, it fell.
The reason may be the different nature of this campaign.
New Zealanders on October 12 will vote under a German-style proportional system and no single party will gain a majority. It is not a simple choice between a government and an opposition.

As TV1 political editor Linda Clark pointed out, with the conservative National Party ranged against Labour, the Alliance and economic nationalist New Zealand First an undecided voter may have rejected the government. Such a voter may be undecided about just which opposition party to back.

Add a slice of the electorate feeling disenfranchised by successive governments pursuing economic reforms they had not campaigned on, and an undoubted improvement in television presentation by Clark under the tutelage of unnamed media trainers.

Then it is easy to understand why Labour has jumped from about 18 percent in the polls to around 25 percent (and to 28 percent according to its own poll tracking) and become easily the highest-polling party of the centre left.
But even that is not the full picture.
Bolger's recent negative campaign warnings of a "crash of 97" and a "Sunday bloody Sunday" if the left wins on Saturday left his business backers with little room to move.
While surveys have shown they undoubtedly favour a National victory they could hardly support such extreme statements and keep faith with their clients and stakeholders.

If the dire warnings had any effect on the left-wing mix it drove voters away from New Zealand First and the Alliance towards the economically more conservative Labour Party and its finance spokesman Michael Cullen, thereby strengthening the appeal of the left to swinging centrist voters.

With New Zealand First yet to pick a coalition partner it is too soon to write the government off. But if it proves the pundits right and opts for Labour, the reasons for National's failure will be easy to find: a poor performance by Bolger, a misreading of the electorate and business's fear of a change and that ugly worm.
